title: Tobin and the Puddle-Scared Hedgehog
markdown:
The moon, like a shiny pearl, peeked from behind the tall Frostcap Mountains. Down below, in a snug little cottage that smelled of sleepy lavender and bubbling brews, young Tobin the wizard hummed a happy tune. A big pot on the fire puffed out soft shimmery mist: his special potion for sweet dreams. Tomorrow was the Starlight Market, and he absolutely, positively needed a very special herb called a moonpetal. With a happy sigh he poured the last bit of shimmery liquid into a tiny bottle with a cork.

“Ready for an adventure, Scruffy?” he whispered. Eyes bright, full of wonder. Scruffy, a hedgehog whose quills were more of a messy tumble than a neat row, blinked his beady eyes from the rug. He gave a little snuffle, a tiny sound that meant all sorts of things. Today Tobin guessed it meant almost. He gently picked him up. Quills tickled his chin.

At the little wooden door Tobin stopped. Right in the middle of the path was a small puddle, catching the moonlight like a tiny fallen star. Scruffy, who usually trotted along happily, froze. Little legs would not move an inch. This was Scruffy’s funny tricky habit: he would not walk through puddles unless you sang to him. And Tobin, who knew lots of spells, had a singing voice that was a bit wobbly. It wobbled up and down like a little bird trying to fly.

“Oh, bother and bluster,” Tobin whispered. The market would be busy soon, smelling of gingerbread and twinkling with early morning stars. He really needed those moonpetals. “Alright, Scruffy,” he said, trying to sound cheerful, hoping to chase away watery worries. “We’ll go through the Whispering Woods. It’s faster, and the path is usually clear.”

The Whispering Woods, just a hop, skip, and a jump from their village, was usually kind and friendly. Moonbeams danced through big old leaves, making wiggly shadows. Because Scruffy was so afraid of puddles, Tobin had to take him the longer way, past the bumpy roots of the oldest oak trees and a cheerful little stream that babbled secrets.

As they got closer, the path, still damp from the night’s dew, got softer and wetter. A few more puddles lay scattered like forgotten mirrors, dark and still. Each one made Scruffy’s quills stand up with worry. Tobin sighed, soft as a breeze through dry leaves. He tried his little song, the one he had made just for this. “Puddles, puddles, go away, Scruffy wants to start the day… no wet toes for splashy play…” It sounded more like a creaky door than a happy tune. Scruffy just dug his little claws into Tobin’s sleeve, a silent no.

A rustling, like dry leaves skittering across stones, came from a patch of ferns. Out popped a small hunched-over figure. Knobbly nose twitching with curiosity. Wide eyes that looked everywhere. Cadogan, a goblin who collected anything that sparkled. Tobin felt a little flutter in his tummy. Goblins, he had heard, could be tricky and liked riddles.

“Hmph,” grumbled Cadogan, voice like pebbles rolling down a hill. “Looking for something, wizard boy? Seen any super shiny stones? Or maybe a lost earring that winks in the moon?” He slumped, shoulders drooping like wilting flowers. “Lost my best button, you see. A really, really pretty shiny blue one. Fell right off my best waistcoat. Gone like smoke.” His shoulders drooped so much the trees around them seemed to sigh with him. Tobin looked at the sad goblin, knobbly fingers tracing the worn cloth of his waistcoat. Then he looked at Scruffy, still trembling by a tempting puddle as dark and still as ink. Cadogan was not trying to be mean. He was just truly, deeply sad.

Then something quite unexpected happened. As Tobin watched Cadogan’s face, full of worry over one little button, he understood how much that small shiny thing meant. In his sadness Cadogan waved his arms, knobbly finger pointing at Tobin’s bag. His hand swept across it, and out tumbled the precious moonpetal herbs Tobin had gathered. Tobin gasped. His own little seed of frustration, planted by the puddles and the late hour, started to grow. But before he could frown, Scruffy, seeing Tobin’s upset, gave a determined snuffle. With a brave wobbly step he walked right through the very edge of the puddle. Quills twitched bravely. Tiny paws made a soft splashing sound. Such a small step. It was a whole journey for a hedgehog.

Tobin blinked. Frustration melted like morning frost. Scruffy was being brave. He looked at Cadogan, who was now peering sadly at the scattered herbs, eyes wide and a little helpless. “It’s all right, Cadogan,” Tobin said, voice soft and calm, like gentle water lapping a quiet shore. “We can find them. Don’t worry.” He remembered a smooth grey stone he had put in his pocket earlier. It caught the moonlight in a special beautiful way, as if it held a tiny piece of the night sky. He pulled it out. “Here,” he offered. “Maybe this will sparkle for you. It’s very pretty in the moonlight.”

Cadogan’s eyes grew wide. His sadness lifted for a moment. He carefully took the stone, turning it over and over in rough dirt-stained fingers. A slow shy smile began to spread, changing his whole look. “Oh,” he said, voice losing its grumbly sound. “It does. It really sparkles. It has the moon’s own twinkle.” He hummed a little goblin tune, a surprisingly happy musical sound that made Tobin smile. “About those herbs,” Cadogan said, sadness gone, replaced by cheerful eagerness. “I have a very good eye for sparkle, you know. Especially after losing my button. I think I saw them tumble over there, by that old hollow log.” And with a surprisingly quick leap for someone so hunched, he pointed right to where the delicate silvery moonpetals lay, safe among the moss and fallen leaves.

As the first hint of dawn painted the sky with soft pink and gold, Tobin and Scruffy walked back to their cottage. The moonpetals were safe in Tobin’s bag, their faint glow a reminder of the unexpected night. Scruffy trotted beside him, still a bit careful of damp spots, but he had walked through a puddle. He had been brave. Tobin hummed a new gentle tune. It was not wobbly at all. It was steady and sweet. The moon, now pale and shy, a faint whisper in the brightening sky, watched them go. At the cottage door another small puddle waited, leftover from the night. Scruffy paused, then took the edge again, one paw, then another, no song required. Tobin bottled the moonpetal last of all, and the dream-potion smelled, just a little, of wet stones and kindness that had not needed to announce itself.
